title: At low Reynolds number flow is a parabola, mixing is diffusion, and curvature and particle size bring inertia back
summary: In a microchannel viscosity wins: the velocity profile is the Hagen-Poiseuille parabola, the pressure drop is linear in flow rate, and streams mix only by diffusion. Bend the channel and Dean vortices appear; add particles and inertial focusing places them on fixed lines.

media.alt: Plot of a mean velocity profile on a logarithmic horizontal axis. Two lines, model A in teal and model B dashed blue, are compared with orange circle markers labelled reference. Model A passes through the markers, model B sits slightly off. A small inset below shows each model's deviation from the reference.
media.caption: Reference render of plot class F10.2 (profile lines against reference data) with synthetic demonstration data, not a project result. The same layout compares a measured microchannel profile with the parabola derived below.

source.note: Standard fluid mechanics (Navier-Stokes, Hagen-Poiseuille, Peclet and Dean numbers, Segre-Silberberg as an observed effect). The figure is the design system's synthetic F10.2 render, so no project number is quoted.

read_the_figure.question: Does the computed or modelled profile match the reference measurement across the channel, and where does it deviate?
read_the_figure.axes: The reference render shows velocity in wall units against distance from the wall on a log axis. For a microchannel the natural version is velocity against position across the channel on linear axes, where the Poiseuille profile is a parabola.
look_at: Markers are the reference (measurement or direct simulation), lines are the models. A model should pass through the markers, not merely near them.
The inset of deviations: a deviation that is systematic (one-signed) is a model error, scatter around zero is noise.
For a laminar channel the profile must be zero at the wall and maximal at the centre. Check this before anything else.
Whether the profile is normalised by the mean velocity: the parabola then peaks at 2 in a pipe and 1.5 between plates.
read_the_figure.proves: A model that follows the reference within the scatter shows it has the right balance of forces across the channel. It does not prove it is right at other Reynolds numbers.
if_wrong: A profile flatter than the parabola: inertia or a developing inlet region, so the flow is not yet fully developed.
A peak shifted off the centre line: curvature (Dean flow) or a gravity or inlet asymmetry.
Non-zero velocity at the wall: slip, which can be real in gas microflows but is usually a boundary-condition error in liquids.
must_check: Axes labelled with units and the normalisation stated (mean velocity or maximum).
Reynolds number, channel shape and distance from the inlet stated.
The measurement method and its resolution near the wall.
A reference line (the exact parabola) shown for comparison.

terms.meaning: The ratio of inertial to viscous forces, $\rho U D/\mu$. Below roughly 2000 pipe flow is laminar.
The diameter of a round pipe with the same area-to-perimeter ratio, used for any cross-section.
The limit in which inertia is negligible and the momentum balance is pressure against viscosity only.
Steady, fully developed laminar flow in a straight round pipe driven by a pressure gradient.
The pressure drop per unit length that drives the flow.
Pressure drop per unit flow rate. For laminar flow it is a constant of the channel, like an electrical resistance.
The ratio of transport by flow to transport by diffusion, $UL/D$.
The measure of how strongly curvature drives a secondary flow in a bent channel; defined from $Re$ and the curvature ratio (definitions differ by a constant).
A circulation in the plane perpendicular to the main flow, such as the two counter-rotating Dean vortices.
The migration of particles in a channel flow to fixed positions across the cross-section, when finite particle Reynolds number gives them inertia (Segre-Silberberg effect).
Reynolds number built on the particle size: it says how much inertia acts on the particle.

remember: $Re=\rho UD_h/\mu$ with $D_h=4A/P$. Microchannels sit at $Re\sim10^{-2}$ to $10^2$.
$Q=\pi G R^4/(8\mu)$ and $\Delta p=128\mu LQ/(\pi D^4)$: halve the diameter and the pressure drop rises sixteen-fold.
$Pe=UL/D$. The channel length needed to mix by diffusion across a width $w$ scales as $Pe\,w$.
Dean number $De=Re\sqrt{D_h/(2R_c)}$ (one common definition). Inertial focusing needs particles that are a non-negligible fraction of the channel and puts them near $0.6R$ in a tube.

understand.title: Intuition
understand.text: Shrink a channel and the viscous force per unit volume grows faster than the inertia, so the flow forgets the past: when the pump stops, the fluid stops. Layers slide past each other in orderly sheets with no turbulence to stir them. Two streams placed side by side stay side by side and mix only as molecules wander across the interface, which is slow. That is both the problem (no mixing) and the opportunity (perfectly predictable flow).

understand.title: What keeps and what breaks the simple picture
understand.text: The parabola and the linear pressure-flow law need a long straight channel and a steady flow. Near the inlet the profile is still developing, so it is flatter. Bend the channel and the fast fluid at the centre, pushed outward by its own inertia, drives a pair of vortices across the channel: weak, but enough to stir streams at moderate Reynolds number. Particles of a size comparable to the channel see inertia even when the fluid hardly does, and they migrate to preferred lines.

understand.title: The hard tier
understand.text: The Hagen-Poiseuille profile is an exact solution of Navier-Stokes because the nonlinear term vanishes identically for straight parallel flow, not because inertia is small: it stays exact at any Reynolds number below transition. Rectangular channels have no closed form, only a series, and the circular-pipe result is a good guide only for aspect ratios near one. Dean flow and inertial focusing are intrinsically inertial: a scaling argument gives their trends, but the equilibrium positions need numerical or asymptotic solution and depend on shape, particle size and Reynolds number.

steps.title: The Reynolds number of a microchannel
steps.note: For a $100\times50\ \mu\mathrm m$ rectangle, $D_h=4\cdot5000/300=66.7\ \mu\mathrm m$. Water at $1\ \mathrm{mm/s}$ in a $100\ \mu\mathrm m$ channel has $Re=10^3\cdot10^{-3}\cdot10^{-4}/10^{-3}=0.1$: far below pipe transition (Reynolds 1883).

steps.note: Scale lengths by $D$, velocities by $U$ and pressure by $\mu U/D$. The convective term gets the factor $Re$ and the viscous term has none. The remaining equation is linear: Stokes flow.

steps.title: Hagen-Poiseuille: solve the axial momentum balance
steps.note: For a straight pipe with steady, fully developed flow the nonlinear term vanishes, so this is exact. The general solution has a $\ln r$ term, removed because the velocity must stay finite on the axis; the constant is fixed by $u(R)=0$. Verified symbolically.

steps.title: Flow rate and the factor of two
steps.note: The centre line moves at twice the mean speed. This is the same $u_\mathrm{max}=2V$ as the atlas example.

steps.title: Pressure drop and hydraulic resistance
steps.tex: \Delta p=G\,L=\frac{8\mu L}{\pi R^4}\,Q=\frac{128\,\mu L}{\pi D^4}\,Q,\qquad R_h=\frac{\Delta p}{Q}
steps.note: Linear in $Q$, like Ohm's law, and proportional to $D^{-4}$. Halving the diameter multiplies the resistance by sixteen, which is why microfluidic pumps need pressure, not flow, to be sized carefully.

steps.title: Wall shear and the friction factor
steps.note: With $G=8\mu V/R^2$ from the previous step, $f\,Re=64$ exactly. Verified symbolically. It is the laminar friction factor in the Moody diagram, valid below transition.

steps.title: A rectangular channel is not a circle
steps.note: Between wide plates the profile is $G\,y(h-y)/2\mu$. For finite width the exact answer is a series, whose leading coefficient is $192/\pi^5=0.627$. I solved the Poisson problem numerically at aspect ratios 1, 2, 4 and 10: the series agrees with it to 1e-4 relative, and the $0.63$ approximation is within 0.2 percent at aspect ratio 2 and better beyond, but off by 12 percent for a square.

steps.title: Mixing is diffusion: the Peclet number
steps.note: With no turbulence, molecules cross the width only by diffusion. For a small molecule, $D\approx10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$, in a $100\ \mu\mathrm m$ channel at $1\ \mathrm{mm/s}$: $Pe=100$, $t=5\ \mathrm s$, $L=5\ \mathrm{mm}$. Large molecules and cells have far smaller $D$ and need centimetres or metres.

steps.title: Curvature gives Dean vortices (scaling)
steps.note: Fluid at the centre is fastest and is thrown outward; slower fluid near the walls returns, closing two counter-rotating loops. This is an order-of-magnitude argument and constants are not derived. The Dean number is the square root of an inertia-times-curvature product; definitions differ by a factor, so always state which one a paper uses. The algebra between the two forms is verified.

steps.title: Inertial focusing: a force balance, qualitatively
steps.note: A particle of radius $a$ in Poiseuille flow feels a shear-gradient lift toward the wall and a wall-induced lift away from it. They balance at a ring about $0.6R$ from the axis in tubes (the Segre-Silberberg observation). The scaling shown is dimensionally consistent (checked) but is a commonly quoted estimate, not derived here. Focusing needs finite $Re_p$ and a long enough channel; at $Re_p\ll1$ particles just follow the streamlines.

worked.title: Pressure drop and Reynolds number in a microtube
worked.problem: Water ($\mu=10^{-3}\ \mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $\rho=1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$) flows at $Q=1\ \mu\mathrm L/\mathrm{min}$ through a round channel of diameter $D=100\ \mu\mathrm m$ and length $L=10\ \mathrm{mm}$. Find the mean velocity, the Reynolds number, the pressure drop and the wall shear stress.

solution.text: Wall shear stress and centre-line speed.

worked.answer: $V=2.12\ \mathrm{mm/s}$, $Re=0.21$ (laminar, deep in the Stokes regime), $\Delta p=68\ \mathrm{Pa}$ (less than 1 mbar), $\tau_w=0.17\ \mathrm{Pa}$. Halving the diameter at the same flow rate would raise $\Delta p$ to about 1.1 kPa. Numbers computed and checked with a script.

analyze.q: The channel diameter is halved at the same flow rate. By what factors do the mean velocity, wall shear stress and pressure drop change?
Two streams enter a $200\ \mu\mathrm m$-wide channel side by side. Explain why doubling the flow rate makes the mixing length longer, and what a designer might do about it.
analyze.hint: $L\propto Pe\,w\propto Uw^2/D$. Think of channel shape and bends.

analyze.q: In a bent channel at $De$ about 10 the Dean flow moves fluid across the channel. Why does that help mixing even though $Re$ is still modest?
analyze.hint: It converts a diffusive length $w$ into a convective path of length of order $w$ in a time of order $w/u_s$.

evaluate.q: A report predicts the pressure drop of a rectangular microchannel, 100 wide by 60 high, using the round-pipe formula with $D_h$. How far off might it be, and what would you use instead?
evaluate.hint: Aspect ratio 1.7: not wide enough for the approximation, so use the series.

evaluate.q: A paper claims inertial focusing at $Re=0.05$. What would you want to see before believing it?
evaluate.hint: Particle size relative to the channel, the particle Reynolds number, and the channel length needed.

create: Design a serpentine channel to mix two aqueous streams in under a second. Which dimensions and which Dean number would you aim for, and what pressure would the pump need?
Sketch the cross-section of a rectangular channel and mark where you would expect particles to focus at moderate $Re$, and where at very low $Re$. State what differs.

checks.q: Why is the velocity profile in a straight pipe a parabola?
checks.hint: Balance of pressure force and viscous force on a thin cylindrical shell.
checks.answer: A steady, fully developed flow has only an axial velocity that depends on radius. The momentum balance is a constant pressure gradient against viscous stress, $G=-\mu\,r^{-1}d(r\,du/dr)/dr$. Integrating twice, with $u$ finite on the axis and zero at the wall, gives $u=G(R^2-r^2)/4\mu$.

checks.q: Water flows at mean speed 1 cm/s in a channel of hydraulic diameter 200 micrometres. What is $Re$?
checks.answer: $Re=1000\cdot0.01\cdot2\times10^{-4}/10^{-3}=2.0$. Laminar, and still low enough for Stokes-like behaviour.

checks.q: At $Re=50$ in a channel of $D_h=100\ \mu\mathrm m$ bent with radius $R_c=1\ \mathrm{mm}$, what is the Dean number, and what does its size say?
checks.answer: $De=50\sqrt{10^{-4}/(2\times10^{-3})}=50\times0.224=11.2$. A Dean number of order ten means a secondary flow that is appreciable compared with the mean flow, and enough to move fluid across the channel several times along a short bend.

checks.q: A group sizes a pump from the pressure drop of the round-tube formula, but the channel is shallow with aspect ratio 20. Is the estimate safe?
checks.hint: Which limit does a very wide channel approach?
checks.answer: At aspect ratio 20 the plate formula $Q=Gh^3w/12\mu$ with the small $0.63h/w$ correction (about 3 percent) is accurate, and the round-tube formula with $D_h$ is not, since it uses the wrong shape factor. Use the plate or series result. The round formula can misestimate the pressure drop by tens of percent.

checks.q: How would you test, without particles, whether a curved microchannel really produces Dean vortices at your operating point?
checks.hint: A dye stream, a cross-section view and a change of flow rate.
checks.answer: Inject two co-flowing streams (one dyed) and image the cross-section downstream of the bend, for example by confocal slices or by outlet splitting. At $De$ below about 1 the interface stays flat. As the flow rate rises the interface should tilt and wind into the two-vortex pattern, and the mixing length should fall. Compare the onset with $De$ rather than with flow rate alone.

Checked with sympy and numerically: Hagen-Poiseuille profile, flow rate, u_max = 2V, pressure drop, f = 64/Re, plate flow, rectangular-channel series against a numerical Poisson solve, Peclet and Dean numbers, worked example. Dean and focusing parts are scaling arguments and are labelled as such; the 0.6R equilibrium and the lift scaling are quoted from the standard qualitative picture, not derived.
